newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece shrugs off Turkish warnings over Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greece shrugs off Turkish warnings over Cyprus.

text.p: Greece on Thursday shrugged off Turkish warnings over Cyprus's plans to buy an anti-aircraft missile system from Russia that has caused concern among Western powers.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis said Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides would be invited to Athens for talks on the issue this month but added there was no cause for concern that a new crisis would erupt between Greece and Turkey.

"There is nothing new in our region. Turkish aggression has been expressed for some time," he told reporters. "We would be playing Turkey's game if we showed particular worry over this and were swept into an atmosphere of crisis."

Simitis was speaking after a meeting with foreign ministry officials on developments after Cyprus announced it would buy a S-300 missile system, which could neutralise Turkish air superiority over the militarily divided island.

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 after a brief Greek Cypriot coup inspired by the military then ruling Athens. Around 30,000 troops are based in north Cyprus, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara.
Turkey has issued a veiled warning about the planned missile purchase.
"What was needed in 1974 and what did we do? We will do the same again. If needed, we will strike," said Turkey's Defence Minister Turhan Tayan on Wednesday.
He said Turkey had no ambitions to grab more land on Cyprus but to protect the Turkish Cypriot minority.
"These threats from Turkey are nothing new," said Cypriot government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides. "We have heard such threats before."
Simitis's statements were similarly dismissive, saying Greece's strength was its composure, insistence on international law and treaties and keeping a steady foreign policy.
He supported Cyprus's decision to boost its defence, saying it had a sovereign right to protect its citizens.
Greece and Cyprus have brushed off criticism and concern by Western allies over possible negative effects of the missiles purchase on efforts to reunite the island in a federation.
They said it was a double standard to worry about a purely defensive system in the south while allowing 30,000 heavily armed Turkish troops in the north.

Washington, which is making a new push for a political settlement, said it will send Carey Cavanaugh, who heads the state department's office of southern European Affairs, to Cyprus on Sunday and Monday to try to reduce tensions.

"Mr. Cavanaugh will come to Athens to meet foreign ministry officials and make his proposals," Simitis said. "If there is something new, we will see if we must change our stance, but I don't see it happening right now."
